# Albright Innovations

> Albright Innovations helps small and medium businesses get more customers and run more smoothly. We manage social media, Facebook and Instagram ads, Google Business Profiles and websites. We set up a 24/7 assistant that answers website and phone enquiries and sends the lead to the owner, and we improve the systems behind the scenes: customer lists, phones, scheduling, quoting, invoicing, follow-up and lead tracking. Based in Big Rapids, Michigan and the Charlotte, North Carolina area, working with businesses anywhere in the U.S.

Tagline: Authentic Influence. Founder: Joshua Albright. Email: joshua@albright-innovations.com. Website: https://albright-innovations.com/

## Services

- [Operations check](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#operations-check): A walk-through of how work moves through your business, from the first call to the final invoice, and where time and leads slip away.
- [A 24/7 assistant for your website and phone](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#assistant): Answers common questions on your website or phone line, takes the customer's details and sends them to you right away, day or night.
- [The right tools for how you work](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#tools): Customer list, scheduling, phones, quoting, invoicing and job tracking, chosen to fit how you work and the tools you already have.
- [Workflows and follow-up](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#workflows): Clear steps from first call to close to follow-up, so nothing depends on someone remembering.
- [Lead tracking and reporting](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#lead-tracking): Working out where your customers come from, so you know which ads, posts and referrals bring in paying work.
- [Social media management](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#social-media): Posts planned, scheduled and answered, so your page stays active without you living on it.
- [Google Business Profile and reviews](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#google-business): Your Google listing kept current, with posts and a steady way of asking for reviews.
- [Social ads](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#social-ads): Facebook and Instagram ads aimed at people near you who are ready to buy.
- [Websites](https://albright-innovations.com/what-we-do/#websites): A clean, current site that tells people who you are, what you do and how to reach you.

## Free tools

- [Where does your week go?](https://albright-innovations.com/#time): Add up the hours you spend on quotes, scheduling, invoicing, retyping and social media, and see what they cost per year.
- [Missed-call calculator](https://albright-innovations.com/#calls): Estimate the jobs and revenue at risk from unanswered calls and slow follow-up.

# Full text of the answers

## How much time do small business owners spend on admin?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/how-much-time-do-small-business-owners-spend-on-admin/

Most owners spend 15 to 20 hours a week on admin. One survey of 251 U.S. business owners put it at 36% of a 45.5-hour week, which works out to about 16 hours.

## What counts as admin

Admin is the work that keeps the business running but isn't the work customers pay for. For most small businesses it looks like this:

- Writing quotes and estimates, and chasing the ones that went quiet

- Scheduling jobs and calling people back

- Sending invoices and following up on late payments

- Typing the same customer details into the phone, the calendar, the quote and the invoice

- Keeping the Facebook page and website current

- Bookkeeping, payroll and paperwork

## What the surveys found

Finding | Who was asked | Source |

36% of the work week goes to admin. With a 45.5-hour average week, that's about 16 hours. | 251 U.S. business owners, September 2023 | Time etc (https://www.timeetc.com/resources/how-to-achieve-more/the-big-price-of-small-tasks-how-entrepreneurs-may-be-unwittingly-keeping-their-businesses-small) |

Most estimates land between 15 and 20 hours a week, depending on the industry and size of the business. | Summary of several surveys | Xero (https://www.xero.com/us/guides/time-tax-small-business/) |

44% of owners hadn't taken a week or more off in the past year where they fully switched off from work. | Same 251 owners | Time etc (https://www.timeetc.com/resources/how-to-achieve-more/the-big-price-of-small-tasks-how-entrepreneurs-may-be-unwittingly-keeping-their-businesses-small) |

## Why it adds up so fast

None of these tasks is big on its own. A quote is twenty minutes. A callback is five. Retyping a customer's address into the invoice is two. The problem is that they happen dozens of times a week, usually in the gaps between real work. Usually only you can do them, because the information lives in your head or your phone.

At 16 hours a week, that's 832 hours a year. If your time is worth $75 an hour, the admin is costing about $62,400 a year, before you count the jobs that slipped while you were doing it.

## How to measure your own week

- For one normal week, jot down the hours you spend on quotes, scheduling, invoicing, retyping and social media. Round numbers are fine.

- Put those numbers into our time calculator (/#time). It adds them up, converts them to hours and dollars a year, and shows which task is the biggest leak.

- Start with that biggest one. Fixing the top task usually frees more time than nibbling at all five.

Sources: Time etc survey of 251 U.S. business owners, 2023 (https://www.timeetc.com/resources/how-to-achieve-more/the-big-price-of-small-tasks-how-entrepreneurs-may-be-unwittingly-keeping-their-businesses-small); Xero, the hidden time tax on small business owners (https://www.xero.com/us/guides/time-tax-small-business/).

## What does a missed call cost a small business?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/what-does-a-missed-call-cost-a-small-business/

A missed call costs you the chance at a job. To put a number on it, multiply the calls you miss by how often a call becomes work, then by your average job value. For a business getting 30 calls a week and missing 40% of them, that's roughly 21 jobs a month at risk.

## The math, in plain words

Three numbers decide what a missed call is worth to you:

- How many calls you miss. Calls a week times the share that go unanswered.

- How often a call becomes a job. If four in ten answered calls turn into work, assume the same for the ones you missed.

- What a job is worth. Your average invoice.

Missed calls times the close rate gives jobs at risk. Jobs at risk times the average job gives revenue at risk.

## A worked example

Input | Example |

Calls a week | 30 |

Share missed | 40%, or 12 calls a week |

Share of calls that become work | 40% |

Average job value | $450 |

Jobs at risk a month | about 21 |

Revenue at risk a year | about $112,000 |

That figure is a ceiling, not a forecast. Some missed callers do try again. The research below suggests fewer do than most owners expect.

## What the research says

- 62% of calls to small businesses went unanswered in a 30-day study of 85 businesses across 58 industries. Only 37.8% were picked up by a person. 411 Locals, 2016 (https://411locals.us/small-business-owners-dont-answer-62-of-phone-calls/)

- More than half of homeowners expect a reply within the hour, and 28% expect one right away. Only about 1 in 5 home service businesses respond that fast. Jobber Home Service Trends Report, 2026 (https://www.getjobber.com/home-service-trends-report/)

- Reaching a new lead within an hour makes you nearly 7 times more likely to qualify it than reaching out an hour later. Harvard Business Review, 2011 (https://hbr.org/2011/03/the-short-life-of-online-sales-leads)

## What to do about it

- Make sure every caller hears back fast. A quick text, a call back, or someone else picking up. What matters is that they hear from you before they call someone else.

- Keep every call in one place. Names, numbers and messages saved where you'll see them, so nothing depends on a sticky note.

- Decide who answers when you can't. A simple rule for who picks up during jobs, after hours and on weekends.

We set all three up as part of the phone piece of an operations check (/answers/what-does-an-operations-check-involve/).

Sources: 411 Locals (https://411locals.us/small-business-owners-dont-answer-62-of-phone-calls/); Jobber (https://www.getjobber.com/home-service-trends-report/); Harvard Business Review (https://hbr.org/2011/03/the-short-life-of-online-sales-leads).

## How fast should I respond to a new lead?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/how-fast-should-i-respond-to-a-new-lead/

Within five minutes if you can, and within the hour at the latest. Reaching a new lead within an hour makes you nearly seven times more likely to qualify it than reaching out an hour later.

## What the research found

Finding | Source |

Firms that reached a new lead within an hour were nearly 7 times as likely to qualify it as firms that reached out an hour later. They were more than 60 times as likely as firms that waited a day. Across 2,241 companies, the average response time was 42 hours, and 23% never responded. | Harvard Business Review, 2011 (https://hbr.org/2011/03/the-short-life-of-online-sales-leads) |

The odds of reaching a lead drop 100 times between a 5-minute response and a 30-minute one. The odds of qualifying it drop 21 times. | InsideSales.com and MIT, Lead Response Management Study, 2007 (https://25649.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na2.net/hub/25649/file-13535879-pdf/docs/mit_study.pdf) |

More than half of homeowners expect a reply within the hour, and 28% expect one right away. Only about 20% of home service businesses respond within the hour. | Jobber Home Service Trends Report, 2026 (https://www.getjobber.com/home-service-trends-report/) |

## Why speed matters so much

A person who just filled out a form or left a message is sitting with the problem in front of them, phone in hand. An hour later they're on to the next thing, or on to the next business. The first company to reply usually gets the conversation, and the conversation is where the job gets decided.

## How to hit it without living on your phone

- A quick reply to missed calls. Even a short message tells the caller you'll be in touch, and buys you the time to call back properly.

- An instant reply to web forms. "Got your message, we'll call you before 5 today." Then make sure someone does.

- Fewer steps between the visit and the quote. When your pricing and wording are already set up, a quote doesn't have to wait for a free evening.

- One place to check for calls, texts and forms. If leads land in five places, some of them wait. If they land in one, the oldest one is always at the top.

- A rule for who answers. During jobs, after hours, on weekends. Written down, so it isn't a daily decision.

This is the first thing we look at in an operations check (/answers/what-does-an-operations-check-involve/), because it's usually the fastest win in the business.

Sources: Harvard Business Review (https://hbr.org/2011/03/the-short-life-of-online-sales-leads); InsideSales.com and MIT (https://25649.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na2.net/hub/25649/file-13535879-pdf/docs/mit_study.pdf); Jobber (https://www.getjobber.com/home-service-trends-report/).

## Do I need a CRM for a small business, and what's the simplest place to start?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/do-i-need-a-crm-for-a-small-business/

If you have more than a few dozen customers, yes, but it doesn't need to be fancy. A CRM is a customer list with the history attached, and the simplest place to start is one shared spreadsheet with six columns.

## What a CRM is, in plain words

CRM stands for customer relationship management, which is a long name for a short idea: one list of everyone you've worked with or quoted, with what happened attached. Who they are, how to reach them, what they asked for, what you quoted, what they paid, and when you last talked.

If that information is currently split between your phone contacts, a notebook, your invoicing app and your memory, you don't have a CRM. You have four partial ones.

## The simplest place to start

A shared spreadsheet with six columns. Nothing to buy, nothing to learn.

Column | What goes in it |

Name | The person, and the business if there is one |

Phone and email | Both, if you have both |

Address | Where the work happens |

How they found you | Referral, Facebook, ad, drive-by. Ask every time. |

Last job and date | What you did and when |

Next step | Quote to send, follow-up due, nothing for now |

Fill it in for every call and every job for a month. That alone will change how you follow up.

## When the spreadsheet stops being enough

- You're typing the same customer into the spreadsheet, the calendar, the quote and the invoice

- Follow-ups depend on someone remembering to look at the "next step" column

- More than one person needs it at the same time, from a phone

- You want to text or email past customers without copying numbers out by hand

At that point the right move is a simple customer-list app that connects to your phones, quoting and invoicing, so a name goes in once and shows up everywhere. There are plenty of good ones. The right one depends on the kind of work you do, and picking it is part of what we do in an operations check (/answers/what-does-an-operations-check-involve/).

## What we'd do

Pick the tool that fits how you already work and move your existing contacts into it. Connect it to your phone and invoicing so it fills itself in, and show your team how to use it in an afternoon. The goal is a list nobody has to maintain by hand.

## How often should a local business post on Facebook?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/how-often-should-a-local-business-post-on-facebook/

At least once a week, so the page looks alive to someone checking you out, and two to three times a week if you want it to bring in work. Consistency matters more than volume.

## Why once a week is the floor

Most people who land on your Facebook page aren't scrolling their feed. They searched for you, or a friend sent them. They look at the last post date before they read anything else. A page that hasn't posted since spring reads as a business that might not be around. A page with a post from this week reads as open and busy.

There's no study we'd stand behind for an exact number, so treat this as a working rule of thumb: weekly keeps you looking alive, and two or three posts a week gives people enough to see you're busy and think of you when they need you.

## What to post

Real work, in plain words. The posts that do best for local businesses are almost never polished.

- A job you finished this week, with a photo and two sentences about it

- Before and after, from the same angle

- A person on your team and what they do

- One useful tip a customer asked you about recently

- A review someone left, with a thank-you

- Hours, holidays, weather closures and other things people actually need to know

## A simple month

Week | Post 1 | Post 2 | Post 3 (if you can) |

1 | Job of the week | Customer review | Quick tip |

2 | Before and after | Meet the team | Hours or an update |

3 | Job of the week | Quick tip | Customer review |

4 | Before and after | Something local you're part of | Job of the week |

## What matters more than frequency

- Answer comments and messages. A question left hanging on a post is worse than no post.

- Keep the basics current. Hours, phone number, address and services on the page itself.

- Sound like yourself. People can tell when a post was written by someone who's never been to the shop.

If the posting isn't happening at all, that's the problem to solve first. Our answer on paying someone to manage it (/answers/is-it-worth-paying-someone-to-manage-our-social-media/) walks through when that makes sense.

## Is it worth paying someone to manage our social media?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/is-it-worth-paying-someone-to-manage-our-social-media/

It's worth it when the hours you'd spend are worth more than the fee, or when the posting isn't happening at all. Three hours a week at $75 an hour is $11,700 a year of your time.

## Do the math on your own time

Posting well takes longer than people expect: taking the photo, writing the words, posting it, answering the comments, and doing that again in three days. Put a number on it.

Your hours a week on social | At $50 an hour | At $75 an hour | At $100 an hour |

2 hours | $5,200 a year | $7,800 a year | $10,400 a year |

3 hours | $7,800 a year | $11,700 a year | $15,600 a year |

5 hours | $13,000 a year | $19,500 a year | $26,000 a year |

If a management fee is less than that number, and the time would go back into work that pays, it's worth it on the hours alone. Our time calculator (/#time) does this with your numbers.

## The other reason: it isn't happening

For a lot of owners the honest answer isn't "I spend three hours a week on it." It's "I meant to, and the last post was in March." In that case the question isn't whether to pay someone. It's whether you want the page working for you at all. A page that posts steadily brings in calls. A page that doesn't costs you the ones who looked and moved on.

## When it's not worth it

- You enjoy it, you're good at it, and you'd do it anyway

- Your customers don't look for you on Facebook or Instagram, and you've checked that rather than assumed it

- The rest of the business can't handle more calls right now

## What to expect from whoever does it

- Posts that sound like your business, built from your real jobs, not stock photos

- A plan you can see ahead of time, so nothing surprises you

- Comments and messages answered, not just posts published

- A short monthly note on what got attention and what brought in calls

That's how we run it. We plan the posts with you, schedule them, answer the comments, and tell you what worked. Here's how often we think a local business should post. (/answers/how-often-should-a-local-business-post-on-facebook/)

## How do I know which ads or posts are bringing in customers?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/how-do-i-know-which-ads-or-posts-bring-in-customers/

Give each ad or post its own trail: a separate phone number, a tagged link, or a "how did you hear about us" that gets written down every single time. Then match each job back to the trail it came in on.

## Three ways to leave a trail

Method | How it works | Effort |

Ask, every time | "How did you hear about us?" on every call and form, written into the customer list. Not asked sometimes. Every time. | None to set up, discipline to keep |

Tracking phone numbers | Each ad, the Facebook page and the website get their own number that forwards to your real one. The report shows which number rang. | An hour to set up, a few dollars a month |

Tagged links | Each post or ad links to your site with a short tag on the end of the address. Your site's reports then show which post sent the visit and whether they filled out the form. | Minutes per post once it's set up |

Do the first one today. Add the other two when you're spending money on ads.

## The step most businesses skip

Knowing where the call came from isn't enough. You need to know where the job came from. That means the source has to travel with the customer from the first call through the quote to the invoice. When it does, you can total up invoices by source at the end of the month and see, in dollars, what each ad or post was worth.

## What a useful report shows

- Calls, messages and forms this month, by source

- How many of each became a quote, and how many became a job

- Revenue by source

- What you spent on each source, so you can see the return

Four lines. If a report has forty, nobody reads it.

## Common mistakes

- Counting likes and reach instead of calls and jobs

- Asking "how did you hear about us" on the form but not on the phone, where most leads come in

- Running three ads to the same phone number, so there's no way to tell them apart

- Judging an ad after a week. Most need a month to show a pattern.

Setting this up is the lead tracking and reporting piece of what we do. We work out with you how the source can follow each customer from the first call to the invoice, using the tools you already have where we can. We keep the report to four lines.

## When is it time to redo my business website?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/when-is-it-time-to-redo-my-business-website/

When it no longer does its three jobs: tell people what you do, show them you're real and current, and make it easy to reach you. If it's more than three years old, awkward on a phone, or shows old hours, prices or photos, it's time to take a hard look.

## The signs

- It's hard to use on a phone: tiny text, pinching to zoom, buttons too small to tap

- The hours, prices, services or photos are out of date, and fixing them means calling someone

- The phone number or contact form isn't on every page

- The photos are stock images instead of your work and your people

- It takes more than a few seconds to load

- It says "2019" somewhere, or looks like it should

- You're a little embarrassed to send people to it

One of these is worth fixing. Two or more, and it's time for a redo. Most people check a business's website before they call. Stanford's research on web credibility found that people judge how trustworthy a site is largely by how it looks. They also trust sites that show signs of being kept current. A dated site doesn't just look old. It costs you the call.

## What doesn't need a full redo

Sometimes the structure is fine and the content is stale. If the site works on a phone, loads fast and is easy to edit, you may not need a rebuild. A round of new photos, current services and an honest "about" page can get you most of the way for much less. We'll tell you if that's your situation. A rebuild you don't need isn't a good deal for either of us.

## What a rebuild involves

- A short conversation about who your customers are and what they need to see to pick up the phone.

- The direction first. We tell you what we'd change and why before anything is built, so there are no surprises.

- The build. Usually a handful of pages: home, services, about, contact, and reviews or gallery. Built to load fast and work on a phone first.

- Your photos, your words. We write it in your voice and use your real work.

- Keeping it current. Small updates on a schedule, so it doesn't drift back to where it started.

We tell you what we'd change before anything is built. Here's what we think a small business site needs on it. (/answers/what-should-a-small-business-website-have-on-it/)

Source: Stanford Web Credibility Project, guidelines (https://credibility.stanford.edu/guidelines).

## What should a small business website have on it?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/what-should-a-small-business-website-have-on-it/

Six things: what you do, where you do it, proof you're real (your photos, your name, your reviews), a way to contact you on every page, current hours and prices where they apply, and a site that works on a phone.

## The six things, explained

- What you do. In the first sentence, in plain words. "Residential plumbing in your town" beats "Solutions for all your plumbing needs."

- Where you do it. The towns and counties you serve, written out. People search by town, and so do the answer tools people use now.

- Proof you're real. Photos of your work and your people, your name, your reviews. Stock photos signal the opposite.

- A way to reach you on every page. Phone number at the top, a short form, and both tappable on a phone.

- Current hours and prices where they apply. If something changes with the season, the site should change with it.

- A site that works on a phone. Most of your visitors are on one. Big text, big buttons, fast loading.

## Page by page

Page | What it needs |

Home | What you do, where, for whom, one photo of real work, and the phone number. Someone should know whether to call within five seconds. |

Services | One short section per service, with what's included and roughly what it costs if you can say. |

About | Who you are, how long you've been at it, why you do it. A photo of you. People hire people. |

Reviews or gallery | Real reviews with first names, or before-and-after photos with a sentence each. |

Contact | Phone, email, address or service area, hours, and a form that takes a minute to fill in. |

## What you can skip

- A blog you won't keep up. An empty blog with two posts from 2021 hurts more than no blog.

- A slideshow at the top. People scroll past them.

- Pages for every tiny variation of a service. Fewer, clearer pages win.

- Pop-ups asking for an email before someone has read a word.

## What we build

Usually five pages, written in your voice, with your photos, built to load fast and read well on a phone. We tell you what we'd change before anything is built, so you see the direction first. Not sure if yours needs redoing? Here are the signs. (/answers/when-is-it-time-to-redo-my-business-website/)

## What does an operations check involve?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/what-does-an-operations-check-involve/

A walk-through of how work moves through your business, from the first call to the final invoice. The operations check takes about 30 minutes, and you get a one-page list of what we'd fix first.

## What we look at

We follow one job through your business and watch where it slows down or depends on someone remembering.

- How leads come in. Phone, Facebook, forms, referrals. Who answers, how fast, and what happens when nobody can.

- Where customer information lives. Phone contacts, a notebook, the invoicing app, your head. How many places the same name gets typed.

- Quotes. How long they take, how they're sent, and what happens if the customer doesn't answer.

- Scheduling. How a job gets on the calendar and how the crew finds out.

- Invoicing and getting paid. When invoices go out, how, and how long you wait.

- Follow-up. Review requests, reminders for repeat work, and reaching past customers.

- The tools you already pay for. Often the fix is connecting what you have, not buying something new.

## What we need from you

- Thirty minutes, by phone, video or at the shop

- A rough idea of calls a week, jobs a month and your average job value. Guesses are fine.

- The names of the tools you use now: phone, calendar, quoting, invoicing, customer list

## What you get

A one-page list, in plain words, of what we'd fix first and why, ordered by what's costing you the most time or the most jobs. It's yours whether or not you hire us. Our time calculator (/#time) shows you where to look first.

## What happens next, if you want it to

We scope the work together and agree on a price before anything starts. Then we build it: the tools picked and connected, the workflows written down, your team shown how to use them. Then we keep it running and show you the results as they come in. Here's how a project runs from start to finish. (/how-we-work/)

## Do you work with businesses anywhere in the country?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/do-you-work-with-businesses-anywhere/

Yes. Based in Big Rapids, Michigan and the Charlotte, North Carolina area, working with businesses anywhere in the U.S. Most of the work happens online, so where you are matters less than what you need.

## What's the same wherever you are

Almost everything. Social media, ads, websites and the 24/7 assistant are built and run online no matter where you are. Setting up and connecting your phones, customer list, quoting and invoicing is done remotely too; we share a screen and work through it together. The operations check happens over a video call, following one job from first call to final invoice the same way we would in person.

## What's different

- Photos for your posts and website come from you or a photographer near you. We'll tell you exactly what to shoot.

- Training your team happens over video, in short sessions.

- We keep normal Eastern time hours. If you're a few time zones away, we'll find an overlap that works.

## Who it's a good fit for

Small and medium businesses that are already busy and want the office side to need less of them: trades, auto, home services, shops with a counter and a phone. Where you are matters less than what you need. Tell us both and we'll give you an honest answer.

## What does it cost to work with Albright Innovations?

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/answers/what-does-it-cost-to-work-with-albright-innovations/

It depends on the scope, and we figure it out together before you commit to anything. The first conversation and the operations check don't cost anything, and you'll have a price in writing before any work starts.

## How we figure it out together

- You tell us what's going on. Through the panel on this site, by email, or on a 30-minute call.

- We do the operations check. We follow a job through your business and come back with a one-page list of what we'd fix first. No charge.

- We pick a starting point. Usually the one or two items on that list that are costing you the most. Not everything at once.

- You get a price in writing. What's included, what it costs, and how long it takes, before anything starts.

## What affects the price

- How much is being set up. Connecting a phone system to a customer list is a smaller job than building the whole first-call-to-invoice workflow.

- Whether it's a project or ongoing. A website rebuild is a project. Running your social media or watching your ads every month is ongoing.

- How many people need training. A two-person shop and a twelve-person crew are different afternoons.

- What you already have. If the tools you pay for now can do the job, we work with them instead of replacing them.

## What you'll always know up front

- The price, before work starts, in writing

- What's included and what isn't

- What we'd do first and what can wait

- How we'll show you results as they come in

We don't guarantee numbers for your business and we don't do pressure. We keep our client list small on purpose, and every deal has to be a fair one for both sides. If a project isn't worth it for you, we'll say so.

## About Joshua Albright | Albright Innovations

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/about/

Home (/) / About

Joshua AlbrightFounder

About
I've built this before. Now I build it for businesses like yours.

I'm Joshua Albright, and I run Albright Innovations. I help a handful of good businesses get more customers and run more smoothly, and I'm involved in every project.

## Where I come from

I grew up around entrepreneurs. My family runs a rental business in Big Rapids, Michigan, now in its third generation, and my mother ran a business of her own. That's where I learned what a small business actually runs on. The phone rings during dinner, quotes get written at the kitchen table, and the owner is the only one who knows where everything is. It's also where I learned that a fair deal is one that works for both sides.

## What I did for twelve years

I earned my marketing degree at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte in 2006. A few years later I started in sales at a startup and stayed twelve years, moving from sales to marketing to contracts to Director of Operations. In that time the company grew to over $10 million a year.

There wasn't much I didn't touch. I rebuilt the company's marketing. I created its contracts department from the ground up and ran it. As Director of Operations I built the full customer workflow, from the first sales call through the close and every follow-up for the life of the contract. I also worked alongside accounting, so the money side and the operations side understood each other.

The part I'm proudest of is the part I'm doing again now. I sit down with the people doing the work, listen to where they want to go, and then build the systems that get them there.

## Why I started this

Because the thing I enjoy most is the relief. A business owner who has been carrying too much, and a few weeks later isn't. The calls get answered, the quotes and invoices go out on time, and the Facebook page looks like the busy business it is. That's why I do this.

## How I work

- I tell you what I'd do with your business and why, before you decide anything.

- I don't guarantee numbers. I show you results as they come in.

- I keep my client list small on purpose, so every client gets my attention.

- I use plain words. If I can't explain it simply, I don't understand it well enough yet.

Based in Big Rapids, Michigan and the Charlotte, North Carolina area, working with businesses anywhere in the U.S.

Reach me at joshua@albright-innovations.com (mailto:joshua@albright-innovations.com), book a 30-minute call (https://calendly.com/jsalbrig-studio/30min), or tell me what's going on.

## Privacy Policy | Albright Innovations

Source: https://albright-innovations.com/privacy/

Home (/) / Privacy Policy

Legal
Privacy Policy

Last updated: October 16, 2026

Your privacy matters to us. This policy explains what information we collect, why we collect it, who we share it with and the choices you have.

## 1. Who we are

This Privacy Policy explains how Joshua Albright, doing business as Albright Innovations ("Albright Innovations," "we," "us," "our"), collects, uses and shares information. It applies to our website at https://albright-innovations.com (https://albright-innovations.com), our landing pages, our forms, our done-for-you services and our 24/7 assistant plans. We are based in Big Rapids, Michigan and the Charlotte, North Carolina area. You can contact us at joshua@albright-innovations.com (mailto:joshua@albright-innovations.com).

## 2. Two kinds of people this covers

People who visit our website, fill out our forms, contact us or buy from us. For this information, we decide how it is used.

People who chat with an assistant that one of our customers has set up on their own website or social pages. Our customer decides what the assistant collects and why. We and our service providers handle that information on the customer’s behalf. If you used an assistant on another business’s website, please read that business’s privacy notice, and contact that business first for any request about your information.

## 3. Information we collect

Information you give us:

- Contact and business details: your name, business name, email address, phone number, business type, area, and your website or Google or Facebook page link.

- Messages you send us and anything else you choose to tell us, including by form, email or chat.

- Account and billing details. Payments are handled by our payment processor (Stripe). We do not store your full card number.

- Content you give us to build your website or set up your assistant, such as text, photos, logos and documents.

Information collected automatically:

- Device and usage information such as your browser, device type, IP address, pages viewed, time on page and referring site.

- Ad and campaign information, such as which ad or link brought you to us (for example, UTM tags and ad-click identifiers).

- Cookies, pixels and similar technologies (see Section 6).

Information from chats with an assistant (for our customers’ visitors):

- The messages typed into the chat, and the name, phone number, email address or other details the visitor chooses to share.

- Basic technical information such as the date, time and page where the chat took place.

- For assistants connected to Facebook or Instagram, the messages and basic profile details Meta passes along to the page owner.

Please do not share sensitive information such as payment card numbers, health information, government ID numbers or passwords in a chat or form.

## 4. How we use information

- Provide, set up, run and support our website, services and assistant plans.

- Respond to your questions and requests, and follow up on forms you submit.

- Process payments, send receipts and manage your account and trial.

- Send service messages such as confirmations, billing notices, outage notices and check-ins about your account.

- Send you marketing about our services, where the law allows. You can opt out at any time (see Section 11).

- Measure and improve our website, ads and services, and understand which ads bring in leads.

- Keep our services secure, prevent fraud and misuse, and follow the law.

- For assistants: deliver chat replies and send leads and alerts to the business that set up the assistant.

## 5. Legal bases and consent

Where the law asks for a legal basis, we rely on our contract with you, our legitimate interest in running and improving our business, your consent where required (for example, for certain cookies or marketing), and legal obligations.

## 6. Cookies, pixels and analytics

We use cookies and similar tools to make our site work, measure traffic and measure our advertising. These include the Meta Pixel, which tells Meta when someone who clicked our Facebook or Instagram ad takes an action on our site, such as submitting a form. Meta may use that information to show you ads and to measure results, under Meta’s own policies. We may also use analytics tools such as Google Analytics.

You can control cookies in your browser settings, and you can manage ad preferences in your Facebook and Instagram settings and through the tools provided by the Digital Advertising Alliance (https://optout.aboutads.info (https://optout.aboutads.info)). Blocking some cookies may affect how our site works. We respond to opt-out preference signals such as Global Privacy Control where the law requires it.

## 7. Who we share information with

We do not sell your personal information. We share it only with:

- Service providers that help us run our business: the assistant platform (our assistant platform provider), payment processing (Stripe), Google (for email, documents, forms and analytics), Meta (Facebook, Instagram and the Pixel), and email, form, scheduling and website hosting tools.

- Language model providers that generate the assistant’s replies. Chat messages are sent to them through the assistant platform so a reply can be produced.

- For assistant chats: the business that set up the assistant.

- Professional advisers such as lawyers, accountants and insurers, when needed.

- Authorities or other parties when the law requires it, or to protect rights, safety and security.

- A buyer or successor if our business is sold or reorganized.

These providers may use the information only to provide services to us and under their own privacy terms.

## 8. How long we keep information

We keep information only as long as we need it for the reasons above, including to meet legal, tax and accounting requirements. Typically that means for as long as you are a customer, plus a reasonable period afterward. Lead and inquiry records that do not turn into customers are kept for a reasonable period and then deleted or anonymized. Chat records for an assistant are kept by the business that runs it for as long as it chooses, and by the assistant platform under its own retention practices.

## 9. Security

We use reasonable safeguards, such as access controls and trusted providers, to protect information. No system is completely secure, so we cannot guarantee absolute security. If a breach affects your information, we will notify you as the law requires.

## 10. Your choices and rights

You can ask us to:

- Tell you what personal information we hold about you and give you a copy.

- Correct information that is wrong.

- Delete your information, subject to legal and business record-keeping needs.

- Stop using your information for marketing.

To make a request, email joshua@albright-innovations.com (mailto:joshua@albright-innovations.com). We may need to confirm who you are first, and we will respond within 45 days (or sooner if the law requires). Depending on where you live, you may have additional rights under your state’s privacy law, including the right to appeal our decision. We will not treat you differently for using your rights. If your request is about an assistant chat on another business’s site, we may refer you to that business.

## 11. Marketing messages

If you give us your email address or phone number, we may contact you about your inquiry and our services. Each marketing email has an unsubscribe link. You can also reply STOP to a text message or email us to opt out. We will still send you messages about your account and billing.

## 12. Children

Our website and services are meant for businesses and are not directed to children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. If you believe a child has given us information, please email us and we will delete it.

## 13. Where information is stored

We and our providers are based mainly in the United States, and your information may be processed and stored here. If you use our services from outside the United States, you understand that your information will be transferred to the United States.

## 14. Links to other sites

Our website may link to other websites, such as Facebook, Google and Stripe. We do not control them and are not responsible for their privacy practices.

## 15. Changes to this policy

We may update this policy from time to time. We will post the new version here with a new "last updated" date. If a change is significant, we will tell you by email or on our website.

## 16. Contact us

Questions or requests about privacy? Email joshua@albright-innovations.com (mailto:joshua@albright-innovations.com).

## 2. Our services

Website and done-for-you services. We build and manage websites, social media, Google Business Profile and operations help for small businesses. The scope, price and timing of that work are set out in a separate written order or agreement with you. If that agreement conflicts with these Terms, the agreement controls for that work.

Assistant Plans. We offer month-to-month plans that let you set up a 24/7 assistant on your own website. The assistant answers your visitors’ questions day and night. Depending on your plan, it can also capture leads and send you alerts, or chat on your Facebook and Instagram pages. The plan names and what each includes are shown when you sign up. The assistant software is run on our behalf by a third-party platform (see Section 9).

Self-serve means you set the assistant up yourself using our step-by-step guide. We offer an optional paid guided setup session, which is a one-time, 60-minute session for one assistant, with no follow-up calls.

## 3. Who can use our services

Our services are for business use. You must be able to form a binding contract and must give us accurate information when you sign up. If you sign up for a business, you confirm that you have the authority to accept these Terms for it.

## 4. Plans, billing and cancellation

- Month to month. Assistant Plans renew automatically each month until you cancel. There is no long-term contract.

- Price. The price is shown at checkout before you pay. We may change prices with at least 30 days’ notice by email. The new price applies at your next renewal after the notice period.

- Free trial. If a plan includes a 7-day free trial, a payment card is required to start it. Unless you cancel before the trial ends, your card is charged the plan price automatically when the trial ends, and then each month.

- Cancelling. You can cancel at any time through your account, or by emailing joshua@albright-innovations.com (mailto:joshua@albright-innovations.com). Cancelling stops the next charge. Your plan stays active through the end of the month you have already paid for.

- No refunds. All payments are final, and we do not give refunds or credits for partial months, unused time or unused messages.

- Included messages and extra usage. Each plan includes a monthly amount of assistant messages. Usage beyond what your plan includes is paid from a prepaid balance (wallet) in your account on the assistant platform. That balance can be topped up automatically from your payment card. Extra usage is billed at the rate shown in your account.

- Payments and taxes. Payments are processed by third-party payment providers. You are responsible for any applicable taxes. If a payment fails, we may suspend your plan until it is resolved.

If you believe you were charged in error, email us within 30 days of the charge and we will look into it promptly.

Support depends on your plan.

## 6. Your responsibilities for your assistant

You are in charge of your assistant and what it says. You agree to:

### Workflows and follow-up

What it isWriting down how work moves through your business, from the first call to the close to the follow-up, so it doesn't live only in your head.
What you getClear steps your team can follow, a plan for following up after quotes and jobs, and fewer questions that only you can answer.
A good fit ifNothing moves when you're off the clock, or follow-up happens only when someone remembers.

-

### Lead tracking and reporting

What it isWorking out where your customers come from, so you know which ads, posts and referrals bring in paying work.
What you getA short, regular report with the few numbers you care about, built from the tools you already use wherever we can. How it works. (/answers/how-do-i-know-which-ads-or-posts-bring-in-customers/)
A good fit ifYou're spending money on ads and can't say which ones pay for themselves.

## Authentic Influence

Being found by the people around you. If customers don't see you online, or what they see looks out of date, start here.

### Social media management

What it isWe plan your posts, write them in your voice, schedule them and answer comments.
What you getA page that stays active and looks like the busy business you are, built from your real work and your real people, without you living on it.
A good fit ifYour page hasn't had a new post in months, or posting is the job that always slides. Is it worth paying someone? (/answers/is-it-worth-paying-someone-to-manage-our-social-media/)

### Google Business Profile and reviews

What it isYour listing on Google, kept complete and current, with regular posts and a steady way of asking happy customers for reviews.
What you getShowing up when people nearby search for what you do, and replies to reviews in your voice.
A good fit ifPeople search for your trade near you and someone else's listing comes up first.

### Social ads

What it isFacebook and Instagram ads aimed at people near you who are likely to need what you offer.
What you getAds set up and watched for you, with plain reporting on what they bring in. We don't guarantee numbers; we show you the results as they come in.
A good fit ifYou've tried boosting posts and couldn't tell whether it worked.

### Websites

What it isA new site, or a refresh of the one you have, that says who you are, what you do and how to reach you.
What you getA clean, current site that works on a phone, kept up to date after it launches. If you'd like, we host it for you with the assistant built in.
A good fit ifYour site hasn't changed in years, or you don't have one yet. What a small business site needs. (/answers/what-should-a-small-business-website-have-on-it/)

## Both sides, together

You can start with one side and add the other later. When we look after both, one team sees the whole business, from the first post a customer sees to the final invoice. The marketing brings in work the office is ready to handle.

## What we don't do

- We don't promise numbers. We show you the results as they come in.

- We don't make you switch tools that already work for you.

- We don't take on more clients than we can look after well.
